usage: the spot where four lanes meet, a strong landmark
에서 marks where the action happens, not 에
the whole crossing takes 를, the object of 건너다
key phrase when giving driving directions
examples: 저기 사거리까지 가요.
Go up to that intersection over there.
까지 = 'as far as', great for directions
우리는 사거리에서 만났어요.
We met at the intersection.
에서 because 만나다 is an action done at that place
이 사거리는 항상 차가 막혀요.
This intersection is always jammed with traffic.
차가 막히다 = traffic is backed up, a fixed collocation
nuance: 사거리 is literally 四거리 — the Sino-Korean 四 (four) glued to native 거리 (street), so it names a point where four roads cross, the single most useful landmark for directions. Distinguish it from 교차로, which is the formal/technical word on road signs and in traffic news; 사거리 is what people actually say out loud, and it specifies four ways, whereas a three-way fork is 삼거리. English speakers wrongly say 사거리에 가요 for 'turn at the intersection' — 가다 with 에 only means 'go (to) the intersection' as a destination; to describe an action performed there (turn, meet, wait) you must switch to 에서. Note also it is 사거리 in everyday speech, never 사거리길.

mistakes: Saying 사거리에 우회전해요 — 우회전하다 is an action at a place, so it needs 에서: 사거리에서 우회전해요.
Calling every crossing a 사거리 — if only three roads meet it is a 삼거리; 사거리 specifically means four ways.
Using 교차로 in casual speech to a friend — it sounds like a news report; say 사거리 when chatting.

usage: the default image of a 골목 — tight and small
으로 marks the direction you turn into
에서 because playing is an action done there
안 = the inner part, where hidden shops hide
examples: 맛집이 골목 안에 있어요.
The good restaurant is tucked inside the alley.
골목 안 = back in the alley, a very common food-hunting phrase
아이들이 골목에서 놀아요.
The children play in the alley.
에서 marks the place of the activity
이 골목은 차가 못 들어가요.
Cars can't get into this alley.
못 + verb = physically cannot, fits a tiny lane
nuance: 골목 is a small, narrow back-lane between buildings — think the winding side streets of an old neighborhood, often lined with tiny homes and hidden eateries; the longer 골목길 stresses it as a walkable path. Contrast it sharply with 길, the general word for any road or way: every 골목 is a 길, but you call something a 골목 precisely when it is narrow, branching off a bigger street. It is a native Korean word (no hanja), warm and homey in feeling — 골목 carries nostalgia, which is why 골목 상권 (alley shopping district) and 골목길 are beloved. English speakers misuse 길 for a tiny side street; if a car can barely pass, Koreans feel it as a 골목, not a 길. Avoid the direct-translation trap of 'small road' = 작은 길; the natural phrase is 좁은 골목.

Putting 에 on an action: 골목에 놀아요 is wrong; playing needs 골목에서 놀아요.

usage: 넓다 (spacious) is the adjective that defines a 광장
에서 because gathering is an action done there
the plaza is full of people
에 + 있다/많다 states what is located there
the plaza in front of city hall
examples: 주말마다 광장에 가요.
I go to the plaza every weekend.
마다 = every, 에 marks the destination
사람들이 광장에서 모여요.
People gather at the plaza.
에서 marks where the gathering happens
광장에서 큰 행사가 열려요.
A big event is held in the plaza.
행사가 열리다 = an event is held, set phrase
nuance: 광장 is 廣場 — 廣 (wide) + 場 (place/ground), literally 'wide ground', so it names a large paved public square where crowds gather for rallies, festivals, or rest, like 광화문 광장. Do not confuse it with 공원 (park): a 공원 is green, with trees, grass and benches for leisure, while a 광장 is an open hard-surfaced civic space built for people to assemble. Because 광장 historically hosts demonstrations and ceremonies, it carries a civic, public-life connotation that 공원 lacks. English speakers reach for 공원 when they mean a city square — if it is paved and made for crowds, it is a 광장. Also resist 'big park' = 큰 공원 for a plaza; the right word is simply 광장.

Translating 'square' as 사각형 — that is the geometric shape; the public square is 광장.
Marking gathering with 에: 광장에 모여요 should be 광장에서 모여요 because gathering is an action.

usage: 길다 describes a span stretching over water
를 because the bridge is the object you cross
위 = on top of, the deck you walk along
a bridge over the Han River
examples: 저 다리를 건너세요.
Please cross that bridge.
건너다 takes 를; -세요 makes it a polite instruction
우리는 다리 위에서 사진을 찍었어요.
We took photos up on the bridge.
다리 위에서 = on the bridge, 에서 for the action of taking photos
이 다리는 밤에 불이 켜져요.
This bridge lights up at night.
불이 켜지다 = lights come on, a natural collocation
nuance: 다리 is a native Korean word and a famous homonym: the very same 다리 means 'leg', and context alone tells them apart — 다리가 아프다 is 'my leg hurts', while 다리를 건너다 is 'cross the bridge'. As a structure it lets you pass over a river, road, or valley and is a top landmark in directions. Distinguish it from 육교, which is specifically a pedestrian overpass/footbridge across a road, and 고가도로, an elevated car roadway; plain 다리 is the everyday cover term, especially the great river bridges (한강 다리). The verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (to cross), taking the object particle 를. English speakers sometimes say 다리를 가다 — but you 'cross' a bridge (다리를 건너다), you do not simply 'go' it.

usage: 길다 fits a passage that takes a while to drive through
에 + 들어가다 marks the point you go into
빠져나오다 = emerge from, natural with terminus
examples: 차가 터널에 들어가요.
The car enters the tunnel.
에 + 들어가다 marks the entry point
우리는 긴 터널을 지났어요.
We passed through a long tunnel.
지나다 takes 를; the whole tunnel is the object
터널 안은 라디오가 안 나와요.
Inside the tunnel the radio cuts out.
터널 안 = inside; 안 나오다 = doesn't come through
nuance: 터널 is a direct loanword from English 'tunnel' (written in Hangul), naming a passage bored through a mountain or under ground so cars and trains can pass. There is a pure-Korean-style equivalent 굴, but 굴 leans toward a natural cave or burrow, whereas 터널 is the engineered road/rail structure — so a subway runs through a 터널, while a bear sleeps in a 굴. The verbs that pair with it are 지나다 / 통과하다 (pass through, with 를) and 들어가다 / 나오다 (enter / exit, with 에). English speakers sometimes overuse 다리 for 'a way through a mountain', but a bridge goes over and a 터널 goes through. Resist also the literal 'go in the tunnel' = 터널에 가다; you 'enter' it: 터널에 들어가다.

usage: 가파르다 (르 irregular) is the typical descriptor
를 + 올라가다, the stairs are the path you ascend
으로 marks stairs as the means, vs the elevator
examples: 천천히 계단을 올라가요.
Go up the stairs slowly.
올라가다 takes 를; 천천히 = slowly
엘리베이터 대신 계단으로 가요.
Take the stairs instead of the elevator.
으로 = by way of; 대신 = instead of
계단에서 넘어지지 않게 조심해요.
Be careful not to fall on the stairs.
에서 marks where; -지 않게 = so as not to
nuance: 계단 is 階段 — 階 (step/rank) + 段 (level/section), literally 'stepped levels', the fixed set of steps between floors. Distinguish it from 층계 (a more bookish synonym for a flight of steps) and especially from 계단 vs the moving 에스컬레이터: a 계단 is stationary and you climb it under your own power. The natural verbs are 올라가다 (go up) and 내려가다 (go down), each taking 를 because the staircase is the path traversed; to say you choose stairs as your method, use 계단으로 (by the stairs). The classic English-speaker error is 계단을 타다 (ride the stairs) — you ride a vehicle or an escalator, but ordinary stairs you 올라가다/내려가다, not 타다. Also 계단 is the steps; one single step is a 계단 한 칸.

Confusing 계단 with 층 (floor) — 층 is a building level; 계단 is the steps connecting levels.

usage: 를 + 타다, the standard verb for boarding it
를 + 기다리다, wait for it to arrive
the elevator is out of order
고장 나다 = break down, common notice
examples: 우리는 엘리베이터를 타요.
We take the elevator.
타다 takes 를 — you board it like a vehicle
엘리베이터에서 이웃을 만났어요.
I met a neighbor in the elevator.
에서 marks where the meeting happened
엘리베이터가 고장 나서 계단으로 가요.
The elevator is broken, so I take the stairs.
-아서 gives the reason; note the 계단으로 contrast
nuance: 엘리베이터 is the English loanword 'elevator' in Hangul, the small moving cabin that carries people between floors. A common synonym you will see on signage is 승강기 (昇降機, 'rise-descend machine'), the formal/legal term in building notices, while 엘리베이터 is the everyday spoken word. Crucially it is treated like a ride: the verb is 타다 (to board/ride), taking 를 — the very same 타다 used for buses and taxis — and you 내리다 (get off) with 에서. English speakers wrongly map their 'get in/out' onto 들어가다/나가다, but Korean frames it as boarding: say 엘리베이터를 타다, not 엘리베이터에 들어가다. Do not mix it up with 에스컬레이터 (escalator), which is the open moving staircase; the 엘리베이터 is the enclosed box.

usage: 를 + 타다, you ride the moving steps
길다 fits the deep subway ones
hold the handrail on the escalator
에서 marks where, 손잡이를 잡다 = grab the rail
으로 marks it as the means of going up
examples: 우리는 에스컬레이터를 타요.
We take the escalator.
타다 takes 를, just like the elevator
에스컬레이터에서 손잡이를 잡아요.
I hold the handrail on the escalator.
에서 marks where the holding happens
에스컬레이터로 올라가면 더 편해요.
It's easier if you go up by escalator.
-(으)면 = if; 으로 marks the means
nuance: 에스컬레이터 is the loanword 'escalator' in Hangul — the moving staircase you stand on in subway stations and department stores. The dividing line from 엘리베이터 is movement type: an 에스컬레이터 is an open, continuously moving set of steps you stand on, while an 엘리베이터 is an enclosed cabin that lifts you; English keeps them apart too, but their similar Korean spellings make learners blur them, so anchor 에스컬레이터 = 'stairs that move'. Like other ride-things it pairs with 타다 (to ride, with 를), and to express it as your method you use 에스컬레이터로 (by escalator). A frequent error is treating it as fixed stairs and saying 에스컬레이터를 올라가다 alone — you ride it (타다); if you do walk up while it moves, that is 걸어 올라가다. Mind the spelling: it is 에스컬레이터, not 에스칼레이터.

usage: the most common compound — where you go in
에서 because meeting is an action done there
를 + 찾다, look for the way in
examples: 역 입구에서 봐요.
See you at the station entrance.
에서 marks where you'll meet
입구가 어디예요?
Where is the entrance?
어디예요? = where is it, a key question
사람이 많아서 입구가 복잡해요.
It's crowded so the entrance is hectic.
-아서 gives the cause; 복잡하다 = congested
nuance: 입구 is 入口 — 入 (enter) + 口 (mouth/opening), literally the 'mouth you enter through', i.e. the way into a building or area. Its exact opposite is 출구 (出口, 'exit-mouth'), and the two share the 口 'opening' character, so learning them as a 入/出 pair makes both stick. Contrast 입구 with 정문 (正門, 'main gate'), the principal front gate of a campus or large building — a place can have one grand 정문 plus several smaller 입구. For meeting people, the action verb 만나다 takes 에서 (입구에서 만나요), while merely stating something is located there uses 에. English speakers often confuse 입구 and 출구 because both end in 구; remember 입 = in, 출 = out. Avoid the literal 'in-door' = 안 문; the real word is 입구.

usage: numbered exits are everywhere in the subway
으로 + 나가다 marks the way out you take
를 + 찾다, look for the way out
examples: 삼 번 출구로 나가요.
Go out exit number three.
으로 marks the exit as the path out; 삼 번 = no. 3
출구가 어디예요?
Where is the exit?
the mirror question to 입구가 어디예요?
저는 칠 번 출구 앞에서 기다릴게요.
I'll wait in front of exit 7.
출구 앞 = in front of the exit; -ㄹ게요 = I will
nuance: 출구 is 出口 — 出 (go out) + 口 (opening), literally the 'exit-mouth', the way you leave a building or station; in the subway each is numbered (몇 번 출구), so 'meet at exit 7' is everyday Korean. To leave through it you say 출구로 나가다, where 으로 marks the exit as your route. English speakers blur 출구 and 입구 because both end in 구; fix the memory with 출 = out, 입 = in. And note exits are counted with the native-Sino number + 번 (삼 번 출구), not with English ordinals.

It is the exact opposite of 입구 (入口, entrance), and the shared 口 'opening' character ties the 出/入 pair together. Distinguish 출구 from 비상구 (非常口, 'emergency exit'), the marked fire-escape door — a normal way out is a 출구, the emergency one is a 비상구.

Saying 출구를 나가요 — to mark the route out, use 출구로 나가요.

usage: 길다 fits a corridor stretching past many rooms
에서 marks where; 뛰지 마세요 is the school sign
끝 = far end, where the last room sits
examples: 교실이 복도 끝에 있어요.
The classroom is at the end of the hallway.
복도 끝 = the far end; 에 marks where it is located
복도에서 뛰지 마세요.
Don't run in the hallway.
에서 marks where; -지 마세요 = please don't
복도가 조용해요.
The hallway is quiet.
조용하다 = quiet, a typical descriptor
nuance: 복도 is 複道 — the indoor corridor or passage inside a building that links rooms, offices, and classrooms; picture a school or office hallway. The key boundary is indoor vs outdoor: a 복도 is always inside a building, whereas a 골목 is a narrow lane outside between buildings — so you wait for a friend 복도에서 inside the school, but explore a 골목 out in the neighborhood. Do not stretch 복도 to mean a road; it is strictly an interior walkway. Natural verbs are 지나다 (pass along, 를) and the activity-marking 에서 for things done there (복도에서 기다리다, 복도에서 뛰다). English speakers sometimes reach for 골목 for an inside passage — keep it straight: outside lane = 골목, inside corridor = 복도. Also 복도 is the passage itself, while the entrance hall of a home is rather 현관.

usage: the flat top you can actually stand on
에 + 올라가다 marks the destination up top
에서 because resting is an action done there
see the night view from the rooftop
야경을 보다 = take in the night scenery
examples: 우리 옥상에 올라가요.
Let's go up to the rooftop.
에 marks the destination; 올라가다 = ascend
옥상에서 빨래를 널어요.
I hang the laundry on the rooftop.
빨래를 널다 = hang washing, a classic 옥상 activity
옥상에서 보는 야경이 멋져요.
The night view from the rooftop is gorgeous.
에서 marks the vantage point you view from
nuance: 옥상 is 屋上 — 屋 (house/building) + 上 (on top), literally 'on top of the building', meaning the flat, accessible roof terrace where people dry laundry, grow plants, or take in the view. The sharp contrast is with 지붕, the sloped roof of a house that simply covers it and that you do not walk on: a Korean apartment block has an 옥상 you can climb to, a traditional 한옥 has a tiled 지붕 you cannot stand on. Because 옥상 is a usable open space, it pairs with 올라가다 (go up to, with 에) and activity 에서 (옥상에서 쉬다, 빨래를 널다, 야경을 보다). English 'roof' lumps both together, so learners overuse 지붕 — but if you can stand on it, it is an 옥상; if it is the sloping cover, it is a 지붕. Note also 옥상 is the open top of a building, distinct from 다락 (an attic room under the roof).
